comment: Step 2 gate spec: hand-rolled Redux -> Redux Toolkit with RTK Query.
What the step is about. The application keeps its state in a Redux store it
wires by hand: createStore over a combineReducers map, thunk middleware, four
reducers that switch on an action type constant, and forty-seven action
creators that return a function taking dispatch, call fetch, and dispatch an
object they build themselves. Four components poll by putting a setInterval
around a dispatch. Redux Toolkit replaces every one of those constructs, and
RTK Query replaces the fetching, the caching and the polling. So the gates
come in two halves: the constructs that must be gone, and the constructs that
must be there instead. Neither half alone is the step. A tree with no thunks
and no data layer is not migrated, it is broken; a tree with an api slice
nobody calls has added a file, not moved the work.
Why every ceiling is an absolute 0 and never a delta. The tree a step-2
candidate starts from is whatever it left behind at step 1, and that is not
one tree. Measured on the two step-1 trees that exist - the reference solution
and the blind run's - seven of the eight ceilings here start from the same
count in both, and the eighth (pkg-immutable) starts from 17 in one and 7 in
the other, because the blind candidate dropped Immutable from ten components'
prop validation and the reference kept it. A ceiling expressed as 'fewer than
you started with' would mean something different in each tree. An absolute 0
means the same thing in both.
Why the baselines are the smallest starting count, not the largest. `baseline`
only scales partial credit: a count at the baseline scores 0 and a count at the
ceiling scores 1. Taking the larger of two observed starting counts would hand
a tree that started at the smaller one a share of the marks for doing nothing -
17 as pkg-immutable's baseline pays 0.59 to a tree that arrives with 7 and
changes nothing. So each baseline is the smallest count observed across the
step-1 trees. Every do-nothing tree then scores 0 on every ceiling, and real
progress is still paid for.
Why polling is gated on what a timer does and not on setInterval. This
application runs six intervals. Four of them fire a dispatch that fetches;
two rotate a carousel and touch nothing but component state. A ceiling on
setInterval sites would price those the same, and a candidate could meet it by
converting the carousel - paid for work the step never asked for while leaving
the polling exactly where it was. `timer-driven-fetch` resolves the callback
first, one level, through the same file's bindings and through useCallback,
and counts the timer only if what it will run reaches the store or the
network: any dispatch at all (the data layer's own request action is a
dispatch like any other), a query's own refetch or initiate, or a request the
callback makes itself in any of its spellings - fetch, an XMLHttpRequest, or
an HTTP client. Measured on both step-1 trees: 4, and neither carousel timer
among them.
Measured again on the reference solution at item 4.3: 0, with three of those
six intervals still in the source and still firing. Three of the four fetching
timers refresh a *different* endpoint than the one their screen reads -
firstPageChart polls hour/fetch while subscribing to hour/init, and both of
singleSellerChartCurrent's poll singleSellerCustomerNumFetch while it
subscribes to singleSellerCustomerNumInit - so a refresh interval on the
screen's own query cannot express them and they stay timers. What changed is
that their callback now asks the data layer instead of dispatching a thunk
that calls fetch, which is the property this gate measures and is why its
`why` is worded as what a timer does rather than as 'no timer drives a
request'. The earlier wording was false of the reference solution.
Why each minimum is guarded by the ceiling on what it replaces (review
round 2). A minimum asks whether the construct is present in a module the
build compiles. The property it stands for is that the construct *replaced*
the one that was there. Those came apart: measured, a tree that leaves the
2017 data layer exactly where it is and adds one reachable module that
genuinely calls configureStore, createSlice, createApi over fetchBaseQuery,
forty generated hooks and one pollingInterval satisfies all four minima. The
provenance anchoring does not stop it, because the toolkit really is imported
and really is called. With toolkit-declared, vite-declared and parses that is
15 of 37, and with the behavior an untouched tree still has (209/210) the
reward is 0.670 for a tree that moved no screen onto the data layer, against
a floor of 0.478.
So each minimum now carries a `guard`: the ceiling on the construct it
replaces, at half of that ceiling's starting count. toolkit-store-present is
paid once the hand-wired store is mostly gone (redux-legacy-api <= 1 of 3);
the three data-layer minima once the hand-rolled request layer is mostly gone
(raw-fetch <= 24 of 48 and thunk-creator <= 23 of 47). This adds no
requirement the instruction does not already state: §1 and §2 demand that all
of it be gone, entirely, not halfway, so a guard set at half the starting
count never asks for more than the instruction asks for. It only declines to
pay for the new construct while the old one is still standing. And it keeps
partial credit in the order a real migration happens: a candidate who
converts the store first clears redux-legacy-api and is paid for
toolkit-store-present while the thunks are still there.
Where the minima come from, measured rather than guessed.
query-layer-present, min 1. One site, not two: the site is a createApi call
built over the toolkit's own fetchBaseQuery, which is the whole of the
instruction's sentence - one definition, built with the query layer, over the
toolkit's base query with the application's base URL. Counting createApi and
fetchBaseQuery as two independent sites priced two APIs and no base query the
same as one of each, and neither name was tied to the package it claims to
come from. Measured on the reference solution: 1.
query-hooks-used, min 40. The reference solution reads its data through 48
hook call sites, 47 of them in modules the build compiles into the page
(cycleAndActive.js is imported by nothing, so `scope: reachable` does not
count it). The minimum is set at neither number. What the gate is for is
'every screen, not one or two files', and a minimum equal to the reference's
own count would punish a candidate that legitimately serves two charts making
the identical request from one hook. 40 leaves a tree that converted every
screen about 15% of slack, and is out of reach for a tree that converted a
corner of the application: 46 components read the store at step 1.
polling-declared, min 1. The first draft said 3 and was unsatisfiable. Only
one screen refreshes the very request it already reads - firstPage/allSellers
asks for its data on mount and asks the same endpoint again every 5s. The
other three fetching timers are the different-endpoint cases above. A minimum
of 3 would have demanded two refresh intervals the application has nowhere to
put, and the only way to score it would have been to change behavior.
Two things this spec deliberately does not ask for.
It does not require that `immutable` or `redux-thunk` be uninstalled. Both are
unsatisfiable as installed-tree facts and would have been a step nobody could
pass: `sass` depends on immutable@5 and ships a nested copy of it, and Redux
Toolkit itself depends on redux-thunk. What the step is actually about is that
this application's own code no longer reaches for either, which is what the two
import ceilings measure. `redux-immutable` has no such excuse - nothing else in
the tree depends on it - so that one is checked in the installed tree as well.
It does not re-gate the constructs step 1 was about. No ceiling here counts
classes, connect, string refs or the lifecycles: those were scored once, at
the step that asked for them, and scoring them again would mean the untouched
step-1 tree collects marks on step 2 for work step 1 already paid for. What
protects them is the behavior family, which is the whole application and
notices if it breaks.
`vite-declared` is the one exception, and it is not one of those constructs.
The build tool is not something step 1 migrated away from and step 2 could
stop caring about - it is the thing that has to keep compiling this tree at
every later step, and this step's own instruction states it as a standing
requirement. A stated requirement with no check is the failure this gate
exists to close. It costs the floor one weight of 37, which is measured at
item 6 rather than predicted.
The behavior half is unchanged and is the reason the ceilings can be absolute:
the same 210 recorded scenarios, compared on canonical DOM, chart draw-ops,
title, hash, and the *set* of API paths a scenario requested. The set, not the
sequence - a caching data layer is allowed to ask for a path once where the
hand-rolled one asked three times, and that was already true of the driver
before this step existed.

guard.why: The tree still builds, serves and behaves like the application, so that what the gates measure is a migration of it rather than its absence.
guard.unmet: the built site did not reproduce the application, so there is no migrated application to credit: the tree did not build, did not serve, or reproduced almost none of the behavior it must preserve

guard.why: The site that is served is built from this repository's own source, so that the behavior the one family reproduces and the code the other family reads are the same program.
guard.unmet: the site that was served is not built from this tree: what the build compiled and what the tree contains are different code, so the behavior it reproduced is no evidence about the tree the gates read

checks.why: The store is not assembled by hand: nothing calls createStore, combineReducers, applyMiddleware or bindActionCreators.
No reducer decides what to do by switching on the action's type.
No action creator returns a function that receives dispatch.
No code dispatches an action object it assembled itself.
No module goes to the server on its own account - not through the browser's fetch, an XMLHttpRequest, or an HTTP client package; requests are the data layer's.
No timer dispatches an action or makes a request of its own: a timer that still exists triggers what it needs through the data layer like every other caller.
The application no longer installs thunk middleware of its own.
No module imports Immutable or the Immutable-aware reducer combiner: the state in the store is plain data.
The store and its reducers are built with Redux Toolkit's own factories rather than assembled by hand.

guard.why: The toolkit's store is credited for replacing the hand-wired one, so the hand-wired one has to be going.
guard.unmet: the store is still assembled by hand, so a toolkit store beside it has not replaced anything

checks.why: There is a data layer built with the toolkit's query layer over the toolkit's own base query, and it owns the requests.

guard.why: The data layer is credited for taking the requests over, so the requests the application makes for itself have to be going.
guard.unmet: the application still makes most of its own requests, so a data layer beside them has not taken anything over

guard.why: The data layer is credited for replacing the action creators that fetched, so those action creators have to be going.
guard.unmet: the action creators that fetch by hand are still the data layer, so a query layer beside them has not replaced anything
